Far Country
fahr KUN-tree
noun phrase
From the Greek ch&omacr;ra makra, “a distant region,” the place to which the prodigal son journeyed and wasted his substance with riotous living.

📖 Biblical Definition

The far country is the distant land into which the younger son of the parable journeyed, when he had gathered all together and took his way from the father’s house, and there wasted his substance with riotous living (Luk 15:13). It is a place named not chiefly by its geography but by its distance from the father, a country far off from the home and the table and the embrace of love. There the prodigal spent all, and when a mighty famine arose in that land, he began to be in want (Luk 15:14). The dictionary marks that the far country is the very figure of the soul’s wandering from God, the self-chosen exile of the sinner who counts the father’s house a prison and liberty a thing to be found afar off. Its near approaches are fair, full of feasting and friends and the brief sweetness of sin; but its end is famine, want, and the swine’s field. The wonder of the parable is that the road into the far country is also the road home, for the same feet that carried the prodigal out carried him back when he came to himself and arose and went to his father. The far country thus preaches both the misery of departure from God and the riches of His grace, who runs to meet the returning sinner while he is yet a great way off, and falls on his neck, and kisses him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The distant land to which the prodigal son journeyed and wasted his substance, a figure of the soul’s wandering from God.

expand to see more

FAR COUNTRY, the distant land into which the prodigal son journeyed in the parable.

There he wasted his substance with riotous living and spent all.

It is named by its distance from the father’s house, not its place.

Its near pleasures end in famine, want, and the swine’s field.

It witnesses to the soul’s self-chosen exile from God, and the way home by grace.

📖 Key Scripture

Luk 15:13 — "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

Luk 15:14 — "And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want."

Isa 53:6 — "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Eph 2:13 — "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A scriptural figure, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the soul’s wandering from God and the grace that brings it home.

expand to see more

The far country is a figure of our Lord’s own teaching, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may know the parable’s far country for what it is, the soul’s departure from the living God, and may trace in it both the misery of sin and the wonder of the Father’s welcome.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true nature of sin as a wandering from the Father into want. He who pictured the prodigal in the far country is the same who runs to meet the returning sinner while he is yet a great way off. The saint who feels the famine of his own departures may remember that the road into the far country is also the road home, and that the Father waits with the best robe and the fatted calf for every son who comes to himself.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek for “a distant region,” the far country names the place of the prodigal’s wandering from the father.

Far Country — Greek ch&omacr;ra makra, “a distant region.”

It is the land into which the prodigal son journeyed.

There he wasted his substance with riotous living.

A mighty famine arose, and he began to be in want.

It figures the soul’s self-chosen exile far off from God.

Usage

"Like the prodigal in the far country, the wandering soul finds the feast of sin ends in famine and the swine’s field."

"The far country is measured not in miles but in distance from the Father’s house and table."

"The same road that carried the sinner out carries him home, where the Father runs to meet him a great way off."
